criteria.title: Requirements and the tension between them

levels.0: Restates 'limit requests' without rules, rejection behaviour or outage behaviour.
levels.1: Lists the rules, the 429 and the latency budget, but treats fleet-wide accuracy and 'the limiter must not take the API down' as unrelated.
levels.2: Per-user and per-key rules, 429 with Retry-After and remaining-count headers, no boundary bursts, fleet-wide limits with a few percent of slack, a 5 ms p99, rules changeable without deploys, and critical rules called out as behaving differently in an outage.

criteria.title: Accuracy versus availability decided up front

levels.0: Assumes limits must be exact and the limiter always available.
levels.1: Mentions that some overshoot may be acceptable, but never says what is sacrificed when the limiter fails.
levels.2: States that a few percent of overshoot buys latency and availability, that durability of counters is not a goal, and that limiter failure degrades limiting, never the API.

criteria.title: Operations per second drive the store

levels.0: No numbers, or sizes the store by memory.
levels.1: Computes 1M requests/s and some Redis node count, but misses that there are two checks per request or never states a per-node assumption.
levels.2: 1M peak and 500k average, 2 rules → 2M script calls/s, a labelled per-primary assumption (50k/s), ρ ≤ 0.5 for single-thread queueing → 80 primaries + 80 replicas, against only ~205 MB of data.

levels.1: Gives a single round-trip figure without the timeout or the parallel checks.
levels.2: Itemises rule match, round trip (cross-zone slower), script time and queueing; runs both checks in parallel; picks a 3 ms timeout inside the 5 ms budget; checks the API fleet at ρ 0.76 with a zone lost.

levels.0: Returns an error with no status code or hint.
levels.1: Returns 429 but no Retry-After or remaining count, or no rules API.
levels.2: 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit (or X-RateLimit-*) headers on every response, a JSON error naming the rule, the in-process check call returning remaining and retry time, and a versioned rules API with shadow mode.

levels.0: A SQL table with one row per request.
levels.1: Redis counters with TTL, but no thought about cluster slots, persistence or why not Memcached or a database.
levels.2: One small hash per identity and rule with TTL of two windows, hash tags explained, Redis chosen for atomic scripts at ~1 ms, persistence off and async replication accepted, rules in Postgres pushed to servers.

levels.0: A box called 'rate limiter' between client and API.
levels.1: Shows API servers and Redis but not where rules come from or what happens on rejection.
levels.2: Walks allowed, rejected (with a local deny cache), rule-change and Redis-down paths across 50 servers in three zones, a Redis Cluster and a rules service.

levels.1: Names several algorithms but not the fixed-window boundary burst or the sliding log's memory cost.
levels.2: Compares fixed window (2× burst), sliding log (exact, ~0.5 MB per busy key), sliding-window counter (2 counters, approximate), token bucket (burst-shaped plans) and leaky bucket (shaping), with a worked estimate, and chooses by the rule's wording and memory.

levels.0: Reads and writes the counter in separate steps.
levels.1: Uses INCR or a Lua script but cannot explain the race or the cluster constraints.
levels.2: Explains the read-modify-write race, why MULTI/EXEC alone is not enough, a Lua script that uses Redis's own clock, does not count rejections, one key per script under hash slots, and the overcount when two rules disagree; handles global hot keys.

criteria.title: Placement and fail open versus closed

levels.0: No timeout on the limiter call; fails closed for everything or never considers failure.
levels.1: Fails open with a timeout but the same way for every rule, or the backstop throttles single-connection users.
levels.2: Sizes a separate service (~51 instances) before choosing an in-process library; 3 ms timeout and per-shard breaker; fail mode per rule (closed for login abuse); a per-key backstop that avoids breaking per-user rules; a failover timeline with detection.

levels.0: One global counter called from every region, or no answer.
levels.1: Per-region limits without stating the overshoot.
levels.2: Rejects a home-region counter on latency (60–150 ms vs 5 ms), counts locally and exchanges counts every second like a grow-only counter, and bounds overshoot (~3.3% for three regions).

levels.1: Lists Redis failure and adding nodes, but not what breaks first at 10×.
levels.2: Covers shard loss, slow shard, full outage, bad rule, clock skew and abusive clients; at 10× names Redis Cluster size and connection count first, with cells, a limiter tier for connection pooling and leases as the fixes; states each decision with its alternative.
